name: Battista Monico
social_status: Peasant, Friuli region, Republic of Venice
biography:
Battista Monico was a Friulian peasant investigated by the Venetian Inquisition in the 1580s as one of the benandanti — those born with the caul who claimed to fight witches in spirit form during the Ember Days. His case is part of the second wave of benandante investigations that followed the pioneering 1575-1580 cases that Carlo Ginzburg analyzed in Night Battles. Monico claimed to battle witches for the protection of harvests using fennel stalks, describing the familiar benandante framework of ecstatic spiritual combat on behalf of the community.

Monico's interrogation records show the characteristic dynamic Ginzburg identified: the peasant subject arriving with a coherent and confident self-understanding as a beneficent spirit-warrior, and the Inquisition's questioning working systematically to reframe this self-understanding within the heretical category of diabolical sabbath attendance. Monico initially described his activities in terms of community service — protecting crops, fighting against the witches who sought to destroy harvests — and showed little understanding of why the Inquisition regarded this as problematic.

The Venetian Inquisition's approach to the benandanti was relatively measured compared to the secular courts of northern Europe: it sought to investigate and correct rather than to execute, and many benandanti survived their encounters with the tribunal. Monico's survival reflects the institutional culture of the Venetian Inquisition, which was less inclined toward execution than many secular courts and more oriented toward penance and reconciliation.
arrest_narrative: Monico was summoned before the Venetian Inquisition in the 1580s following denunciation for claiming benandante identity. He appeared before the Inquisition's tribunal and was questioned about his claimed night journeys and spirit battles.

interrogation_and_confession.initial_response: Claimed benandante identity confidently — fought witches with fennel stalks during Ember Days for crop protection
interrogation_and_confession.final_confession_summary: Described nocturnal battles with fennel stalks against witches armed with sorghum during the four seasonal Ember Days; spirit leaving body while sleeping; assembly of benandanti and witches; harvests' fate determined by battle outcome; maintained that his activities were beneficial to the community

accusations_against_them: Practicing benandante rituals constituting illicit spiritual commerce
historiographical_significance: Monico's case contributes to Ginzburg's reconstruction of benandante belief as a folk practice preceding and distinct from the demonological sabbath framework that the Inquisition sought to impose on it. His confident initial self-presentation as a beneficial spirit-warrior represents the unreformed benandante identity that Ginzburg argues was gradually transformed through repeated inquisitorial questioning across the late sixteenth century. His survival reflects the comparative moderation of the Venetian Inquisition.
source_method: Venetian Inquisition records; analyzed in Carlo Ginzburg's Night Battles (I Benandanti, 1966) and Ecstasies (1991)
